articles.title_orig: Ukraine's Zelenskyy on defying US in attacking Russian oil: 'Our response must be painful'
articles.title_zh: Ukraine's Zelenskyy on defying US in attacking Russian oil: 'Our response must be painful'
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy defended strikes on Russian oil facilities in an exclusive Fox News interview with Trey Yingst, saying Ukraine's response to Moscow's attacks "must be painful."
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is defying calls from the Trump administration for his armed forces to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, telling Fox News: "Our response must be painful."
In an interview in Kyiv, Zelenskyy acknowledged holding discussions with the Trump administration about targeting oil facilities, attacks President Donald Trump has pinned as being partly to blame for high gas prices in the U.S.
"We had different conversations — different, and several — with President Trump and with his team about attacks on refineries," Zelenskyy said.
"We said that if you want us not to attack Russia's refineries, they have not to attack our energy system."
TRUMP TELLS ZELENSKYY TO STOP DOING 'ONE THING' DURING ATTACKS ON RUSSIA
During an interview with Fox News, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged President Donald Trump to pursue an energy cease-fire with Russia as Washington pressures Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries. (Fox News)
Ukraine has reported near-daily Russian strikes on energy infrastructure , triggering power outages just as temperatures dip ahead of winter.
"That's why we have to respond. But our response has to be painful for Russian military people," Zelenskyy said. "If we will not respond on energy, they will continue."
U.S.-Ukraine relations took a further hit in October when Trump struck a deal to import millions of tons of Russian diesel to the United States.
ZELENSKYY ACCUSES PUTIN OF DEFYING TRUMP'S CEASEFIRE PUSH, SENDS POINTED MESSAGE TO WHITE HOUSE
Zelenskyy warned President Donald Trump against helping Russia while praising first lady Melania Trump’s role in securing a humanitarian evacuation from Russian-controlled territory. (Fox News)
Zelenskyy suggested Ukraine might be encouraged to hold off on further attacks on Russian oil facilities if the United States were to deliver more U.S.-made Patriot missile interceptors to protect Ukrainian skies. Pressed by Fox News on whether that might be seen as an attempt to leverage Trump, Zelenskyy said: "I don't have any concerns when I share the truth between partners."
"Our countries are huge partners. American society (is a) huge supporter."
"And that's why I have to share with (the) president the truth, the real situation: that America can't help Russia. (The) president can't help Putin ."
US WILL MEDIATE UPCOMING UKRAINE-RUSSIA TALKS IN ABU DHABI, WITKOFF SAYS
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Fox News that Ukraine will continue targeting Russian oil refineries despite objections from the Trump administration. (Pier Marco Tacca; Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
Ahead of planned peace talks in the United Arab Emirates, Zelenskyy urged Trump to launch another push for a targeted ceasefire where both Russia and Ukraine refrain from attacks on energy facilities.
"If the American president thinks that this war has influence on the prices," Zelenskyy said, "he can ask, energy ceasefire, during (the) Abu Dhabi trilateral meeting: energy ceasefire."
Zelenskyy spoke with Fox News hours before starved and exhausted residents left the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky and crossed into Ukrainian-held territory under a humanitarian truce brokered by first lady Melania Trump , the first of its kind in more than four years of war.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Zelenskyy welcomed the first lady's initiative, calling the evacuations "a huge result," and adding: "I don't know how many such steps will be available for us, but if the first lady can do it ... it's very helpful. I'm very thankful to her."
Trey Yingst currently serves as chief foreign correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in August 2018.

articles.title_orig: 5 iPhone Features You Should Be Using After Updating To iOS 27
articles.title_zh: 5 iPhone Features You Should Be Using After Updating To iOS 27
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27 just made your iPhone a lot more capable.
The iPhone is easy to recommend to anyone looking for great smartphone hardware and long-term software support. The previous few iOS releases, however, have been pretty janky. With iOS 27, Apple therefore shifted its focus to ironing out bugs and improving overall stability rather than cramming in another round of flashy new features, and a good chunk of the WWDC 2026 keynote covered improvements such as snappier app launch times, faster AirDrop transfers and better memory management.
Apple's commitment to software updates also means iOS 27 compatibility extends all the way back to the iPhone 11, which is great news since iOS 26 would have been a terrible final major update to be stuck on. If you haven't already updated your iPhone, you can do so by navigating to Settings > General > Software Update .
Not much has changed visually, which makes sense since Apple only recently overhauled its design language with Liquid Glass. There is now a system-wide transparency slider, though, which many users had been asking about. Reports about battery life are mixed — some say they're getting less screen-on time than before, while others haven't had issues. Personally, iOS 27 has been such a blessing performance-wise on my aging iPhone 15 Pro Max that I'm willing to put up with slightly worse battery life.
Of course, stability upgrades aren't the only thing Apple introduced with iOS 27. The update also brings a handful of useful tidbits, and here are five features you should definitely check out after updating your iPhone.
Apple Intelligence has had a rocky start. After all, it took Apple two whole iOS generations to deliver on its promises of a more capable Siri. Most of the Apple Intelligence suite has been pretty underwhelming, unless you're one of the five people who enjoy generating custom emojis using Genmoji , but iOS 27 changes that. The Shortcuts app has received a major upgrade, and Apple Intelligence might finally have a genuinely useful feature to show for itself.
You've been able to create pretty complex shortcuts and automations on iOS for a while now, and you can even import shortcuts that others have created and shared. iOS 27 now lets you create shortcuts using natural language prompts, which Apple Intelligence handles. When you launch the app and tap the + button, you can start describing the shortcut you want.
In my testing, the integration works pretty well and usually creates straightforward shortcuts without issues. That said, it pieces together the wrong actions sometimes and ends up with a shortcut that doesn't do exactly what you want. Fortunately, you can still manually tweak shortcuts created using Apple Intelligence by tapping Edit .
You can also use Apple Intelligence actions within your shortcuts. Apple currently offers three AI models, including an on-device model for faster processing. You can create shortcuts for actions involving information extraction, summarization or generation of text and documents. The Cloud and Cloud Pro models do have a daily rate limit, though.
The Wallet app on the iPhone stores your payment cards, transit passes, event and cinema tickets, digital keys and more. Until now, users could only add digital passes and credentials if the issuer supported Apple Wallet and provided a compatible pass. While several companies and services offered this convenience, plenty of issuers didn't support it. As a collector, I was a bit disheartened to see my local IMAX theater stop offering Apple Wallet passes for movie tickets.
With iOS 27, you can create custom passes and add them to Apple Wallet. This is extremely handy for those with loyalty cards or gym memberships that don't offer native Apple Wallet support. There are two ways you can create a pass in Apple Wallet, and Apple Intelligence comes in handy again here. On supported iPhone models, you can open an image (or screenshot) of a ticket or membership card with a barcode, swipe up and tap on Add Pass to Wallet .
If this option doesn't show up, you can also open the Wallet app, tap the + icon at the top and select Create a Pass . Tap on Continue and take a photo of the ticket or ID card. The Wallet app will then use Visual Intelligence to extract relevant information from the image and create a pass. If you want to change the pass' details or visuals, tap Edit.
For years, Apple's virtual assistant, Siri, has lagged behind competitors like Google Assistant. Slow responses are forgivable, but Siri would often struggle with even the most basic requests. Apple first promised a major Siri overhaul with iOS 18's Apple Intelligence suite, but it's taken over two years to come to fruition. iOS 27 comes with Siri AI , and users with a compatible iPhone can join the waitlist by navigating to Settings > Siri . The AI-powered virtual assistant is still in beta, but things are already starting to look promising.
Siri now understands and fulfills your requests noticeably better, with a huge improvement in how it handles follow-up queries. Though it still takes a hot second to process most requests, its responses are more relevant, and it doesn't hit you with the "Here's what I found on the web" reply as often. What's more impressive about Siri AI, though, is the fact that it now understands personal context.
It can pull information from your messages, emails, photos and more to answer questions or perform tasks that previously required you to manually dig through different apps. Third-party app support is still limited, but if you mainly use iMessage and the default Mail app on your iPhone, you'll likely find Siri to be one of iOS 27's biggest improvements. The Camera app has a new Siri mode as well, which taps into Visual Intelligence to answer questions about whatever you're pointing your camera at.
The AirPods are some of the most popular wireless earbuds on the market, and they work best when paired with an iPhone, iPad or Mac. Most modern AirPods models support Spatial Audio with head tracking, and several music streaming services like Apple Music and Tidal let you enjoy Dolby Atmos content. Sound quality is also widely regarded as one of their strongest selling points, particularly on the higher-end Pro models like the AirPods Pro 3 that we reviewed. With iOS 27, though, you can finally tweak the sound to your liking using a built-in equalizer.
Apps like Apple Music have long allowed you to apply EQ presets, but the new AirPods equalizer works system-wide. The feature is available on AirPods 4 and newer, AirPods Pro 2 and newer and the AirPods Max 2. Connect your AirPods to your iPhone, launch the Settings app, tap on the AirPods settings at the top of the screen and navigate to Audio & Routing > Equalizer .
The Recommended option is selected by default, which delivers the balanced sound profile you've grown used to. If you tap on Custom , you can manually adjust the lows, mids and highs to your liking. If you prefer thumpy bass, increase the lows slider, but if you want vocals to sound clearer, try bumping up the mids or highs instead. Though Apple is only offering a 3-band equalizer, it's still a welcome addition. My AirPods Pro 2 already deliver punchy lows, but as a basshead, I appreciate having the option to crank up the bass even further.
Apple's latest mobile OS also has several additions that make browsing more convenient. For starters, Safari now lets you set up alerts for webpage changes, so you don't have to check yourself. This is useful if you're tracking a product's price, waiting for tickets to go on sale or keeping an eye on when an out-of-stock item becomes available again.
On your iPhone, launch Safari , head to a webpage you want to track, tap on the icon with three horizontal lines in the address bar and select Notify Me . Since this feature uses Apple Intelligence, you can describe what exactly you want Safari to monitor. You can then choose how frequently Safari checks the webpage for changes.

articles.title_orig: Apple explains the $400 premium for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display
articles.title_zh: Apple explains the $400 premium for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display
articles.content_orig:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
Steve Jobs famously said touch "doesn’t work" on a laptop and is "ergonomically terrible." Yet at Apple’s Pro and Tell event , the company launched a touch-enabled MacBook Pro . PCMag hardware expert Joe Osborne found the touch screen responsive and smooth during his hands-on time, which makes me optimistic that Apple has finally cracked the vertical touch screen.
I've used touch-screen Windows laptops for more than a decade, so I know firsthand which touch features actually matter and which are gimmicks. These are the things I can’t wait to try on a touch-friendly version of macOS . None of them are novel or complex, but they make everyday computing feel far more natural.
I frequently use my Windows laptop's touch screen to sign PDFs and other documents. Placing my finger on the screen and simply drawing my signature is much faster than painstakingly doing so via the touchpad. The Preview app on a Mac is already excellent for filling out and signing documents, and I expect a touch screen to significantly expand its usefulness.
Similarly, I would much rather draw on my MacBook’s screen to annotate documents, create sketches, compose notes, and put together whiteboards than use my mouse. I often feel tempted to scribble notes on a phone or tablet and then copy notes back to my Mac, just because it's currently so inconvenient to do so directly on my laptop.
Unfortunately, the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display doesn’t support the Apple Pencil, so your inputs won't be pressure-sensitive. The screen obviously also doesn’t lie completely flat, so I doubt it will be optimal for long drawing sessions. Apple’s iPad remains the better platform for professional digital art creation by far.
I frequently use my finger to scroll through documents and web pages on my Windows laptop’s touch screen. This ability is particularly useful when I'm using my laptop in awkward or cramped situations, such as on airplanes, where the touchpad is pressed close to my body.
The ability to pinch-to-zoom is excellent for working with large images, documents, and maps. Simply touching a point on the laptop’s screen and then pinching or expanding to zoom in or out is much more intuitive and fluid than doing so on a trackpad. I can't imagine using either my phone or Windows laptop without this feature, so I’m excited to see it come to a future MacBook.
Apple says the touch-enabled display “[brings] pros a whole new way to interact with their content”, and shows off rotating 3D models with touch input in professional apps like Blender. But even average Mac users who don’t engage in professional 3D modeling could appreciate this feature when rotating the globe in Google Earth, for example. Touch gives you much finer control over these types of actions.
Apple’s macOS already runs iPhone and iPad apps. But apps sometimes require alternative touch controls. For example, you might need to press and hold the Option key on your Mac’s keyboard and use the trackpad as a virtual touch screen. I avoid these on my Mac as much as I can because they are confusing and awkward. Actual touch controls will make this experience so much better. Apple also points out that developers can now test the touch experience in their apps directly on their MacBook’s screen during the creation process.
Developers often create modern macOS apps using Apple’s Catalyst or SwiftUI frameworks, which produce a single app that runs across iOS and macOS with similar interfaces. The iPad and Mac versions of some apps often look almost identical. With so many programs already designed for touch input, it’s only natural to let me actually touch and use them as the developer originally intended. With very little modification, I think that many existing Mac apps can work surprisingly well with touch. Apple also has a variety of Apple Arcade games that work on both macOS and iOS, and touch controls are a better fit for some of them.
Apple’s iPhone Mirroring feature lets you see your iPhone screen and interact with it on your Mac’s desktop. Directly touching the screen is obviously more convenient than using a mouse and keyboard to operate my phone. I've been able to do this with a mirrored Android phone on a Windows 11 touch-screen laptop for a while now.
Despite all the conveniences of a touch screen, there's no getting around the fact that it's going to cause smudges. I already regularly wipe my laptop’s screen with a microfiber cloth, so I'll likely need to do it even more often with a touch screen.
Apple's first touch-screen Mac is a pricey machine built for professionals, but the company's announcement makes a point of pitching touch for everyday use, too, promising that "everyday tasks are simple and intuitive." That's a strong hint that touch won’t stay exclusive to the high end for long. Cheaper models might not get the same level of hardware engineering, but in principle, a touch screen makes just as much sense on a $699 MacBook Neo as on a $2,899 MacBook Pro. And if your arm ever feels like it's about to fall off, the trackpad isn't going anywhere.
I've been writing about technology for more than 15 years and using it in earnest for over twice as long. As a member of PCMag's software team, I focus on Windows coverage, but also write about other key desktop operating systems and system apps. (I used Windows 3.1 upon its release and have followed every subsequent release closely).
Prior to joining PCMag, I wrote for How-To Geek starting in 2011, and my articles amassed over a billion page views. I went on to run the publication as editor-in-chief for four and a half years. I have also contributed to Computerworld, Fast Company, PCWorld, Reader's Digest, The New York Times, and many other outlets about everything from AI to PC hardware to Windows. I founded and ran my own direct-to-reader Windows-focused newsletters, Windows Intelligence and The Windows ReadMe, working in partnership with Thurrott.com.

articles.title_orig: Beyond screens: Mercedes-Benz’s new holographic heads-up display
articles.title_zh: Beyond screens: Mercedes-Benz’s new holographic heads-up display
articles.content_orig:
Do screens in cars represent luxury? Judging by the latest car interiors, the answer would seem to be an emphatic “yes.” Screens aren’t just getting larger; they are multiplying across the dashboard and morphing into different forms and concepts. Indeed, an interior’s screens are a pretty good indicator of what brand made the car—or at least how much the owner paid for it.
But is this actually what customers want ? Are more screens really better? And even if they are, luxury car features inevitably trickle down to cheaper, more mainstream offerings, and screens can only get so big. That leaves luxury automakers with another question to answer: “What’s next?”
Mercedes-Benz is working on a new display alternative that could provide an answer. For now, it’s known as the holographic display. Forget the images from Star Trek and Star Wars that just popped into your head, though. It’s effectively a more advanced form of heads-up display, or HUD.
Whereas a traditional HUD projects images onto the windshield glass, the holographic display has two main components. It still uses a projector, but its key element is a special transparent film laminated into the glass. The film uses holographic optical elements, or “super-small mirrors,” as Mercedes development engineer Lena Hees described them, that selectively reflect the light emitted by the projector, keeping the image visible even in direct sunlight while hiding it from the driver’s view.
Today, the passenger-side touchscreens in Mercedes and other luxury vehicles rely on driver-monitoring cameras or screen polarization to keep the driver from seeing what is playing on the passenger side.
Speaking of passenger screens, the holographic display is clearly being considered as a future alternative or replacement for this technology. Although screens in cars are increasingly ubiquitous, a recent JD Power study indicated that car owners classify passenger screens as “ not necessary ” and have generally negative opinions about them. Mercedes has clearly observed similar opinions but for slightly different reasons.
“We have customers who like the Hyperscreen,” said development engineer Maximilian Hilger of the pillar-to-pillar screen found in an increasing number of Mercedes models. “But there are others who want to maintain luxury materials.”
In other words, the massive screen design doesn’t seem as luxurious as the pillar-to-pillar bands of wood or other materials found in previous-generation models. And that’s not an opinion isolated to Mercedes’ customers.
New Mercedes chief design officer Bastian Baudy recently told German magazine Auto Motor Sport that “Materiality and haptics must remain tangible—with switches, buttons, and intuitive controls. Real materials are at the heart of Mercedes: metal, wood.”
Mercedes CEO Ola Källenius went further, grouping interior quality and materials among the brand’s “forever values,” along with safety and maintaining what a Mercedes is like to drive.
That presents conflicting priorities, however.
“Yes, you need to have all the [technology] that a customer could ever dream of and wants,” Källenius told Ars. “But you need to package it in an aesthetically pleasing way. That’s also part of it.”
That brings us back to the holographic display. Keep in mind that the photos in this article show early prototypes I saw at Mercedes’ research facilities in Sindelfingen, Germany. The prototype projector sits inside a rather crude, trapezoidal hole dug into the dash of a right-hand-drive, pre-2027 S-Class. It’s also loud, with a cooling fan whirring like a laptop visiting too many junk-filled websites.
The production version would have a much smaller projector opening than those of the prototype and existing heads-up displays. Manual Holstein, a manager working in Mercedes research for future displays, indicated that the projector could be small enough to be hidden behind wood or metal trim pieces. Holstein also said you won’t hear a fan in the production model and that the resolution would improve.
The resolution is certainly considerably better than any current head-up display, including Mercedes’ own, which features augmented reality elements . Full-color, commercial-like videos of the C-Class Electric played during the demonstration, and the display was sufficiently bright, even though Holstein said the prototype was operating at just 20 percent of its maximum brightness.
Issues remain, however. The resolution may be good compared to the arrows, script, and graphics of a current HUD, but it’s poor when compared to a passenger touchscreen. The video’s contrast was also too high, and as you can see in the photos, the picture was distorted into a narrow height due to the angle of the windshield. Frankly, no one would choose to watch anything on it over a phone, tablet, or conventional passenger screen. It needs to improve by orders of magnitude before becoming a viable alternative.
Again, though, this is just a prototype. Holstein said the holographic film size, or “eyebox,” can be made much bigger and be raised higher than the HUD-like height of the prototype. He also dismissed the distortion as a problem unique to the prototype.
Imagine nearly half the windshield transformed into a virtual screen that’s visible only to the passenger. Beyond videos or other entertainment, Mercedes envisions the holographic display highlighting points of interest in the view through the windshield. A similar display could be placed on the driver side, showing situational information, enabling video calls, or providing entertainment when parked. In the future, it could even let drivers watch things other than the road when Mercedes’ Level 3 autonomous driving system allows them to take their eyes off it. At the very least, the technology could replace today’s HUDs and their larger projector boxes.
Having experienced the prototype while the car was moving, I also think the holographic display could help prevent the motion sickness that can come from staring at a passenger screen while the car is moving. The higher screen angle and ability to see more of the outside world beyond created a notably different visual experience.
Of course, the question remains: “Is this what customers want?”
If the JD Power survey found that customers don’t care about passenger touchscreens, will they be any more enthusiastic about holographic video displays? That seems doubtful. But that’s just as much of an open question as whether the production version will actually live up to its promises.
There’s also another matter: What, exactly, defines luxury? Before Bastian Baudy took over as Mercedes’ chief design officer this year, his predecessor and former boss Gordon Wagener echoed Källenius’ thoughts about the direction of the brand’s interiors. He was considerably blunter, though.
“Screens are not luxury,” Wagener told ABC News . “You have a better—and bigger—TV at home, right? And every car has a big screen. So we have to create luxury beyond the screen. That’s why I talk about craftsmanship and sophistication.”
If the holographic display lets automakers emphasize traditional design and materials while still offering unique technology, it could be a promising way forward.

articles.title_zh: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countries
articles.content_orig:

A number of UK meat suppliers said their fridges heated up overnight as they were impacted by cyber attacks targeting software used by supermarkets and food suppliers across Europe .
The Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (Aims) said a few of its roughly 300 members had “unexpectedly become collateral” from the hack.
Some members saw fridge systems begin to defrost on Monday night, and another saw their unit rise up to 100C in temperature.
But because of the way that abattoirs are typically run, the units were empty at the time – so there was no impact on any food produce.
A spokesman for Aims said: “None who have been affected have lost any meat, but once again this must act as a reminder to all in the food industry, at whatever point in the supply chain they are, that their businesses may be seen by some as targets.”
“We urge our members and the wider industry to be vigilant,” he added.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said it is working with the firms affected and that the national impact is “minimal”.
Speaking at the launch of the NCSC annual report on Tuesday, Paul Chichester, director of operations, said: “We’re aware of those incidents in the UK, and obviously we’re working with the affected organisations. We’ll keep monitoring that.
“At the moment, the impact is minimal.”
He went on: “We’re working with organisations identifying existing vulnerabilities in the UK and trying to get those closed before somebody exploits them.”
It is understood that no major supermarket chain has been directly impacted by the hack.
But retailers are being urged to monitor their systems closely for potential risks and ensure their software is up to date, as well as having contingency plans in place in case food produce needs to be relocated.
Graham Wynn, assistant director of regulatory affairs at the British Retail Consortium , said: “Retailers invest heavily in their cybersecurity and are currently working with the NCSC to ensure their fridges and freezers are secure as possible against potential attacks.”
Rupert Ashby, chief executive of the British Frozen Food Federation, said retailers “across the supply chain are taking cyber security extremely seriously”.
“Members are looking closely at their freezer provision and assessing how vulnerable their systems might be,” he said.
Head of the NCSC Dr Richard Horne said teams had been working throughout the night to alert British firms that are vulnerable to such an attack.
It emerged that the cyber attack on French supermarket fridges involved legacy technology connected to internet with default passwords.
He told an audience at the report launch in central London: “Last night, we had people working through the night contacting organisations that we could see they had vulnerable technology exposed.”
Dr Horne earlier told the BBC Radio 4 Today programme: “There are handfuls of organisations in the UK we’ve alerted and we’re aware of a couple of impacts.”
Speaking about who was behind the attack, he said: “It’s too early for us to say at the moment and give a definitive answer.”
Asked if it reinforces warnings from the Defence Secretary that people in the UK should stockpile, he said: “Absolutely. And we saw criminal attacks last year impact retailers in the UK.
“We know it can happen, and we’ve seen it across Europe.
“We alert people. We intervene where we can. But, at the end of the day, it’s your business. It’s your charity. It’s your life. You need to make the choice and choose wisely.”
The NCSC annual report said that its incident management team received 1,831 reports this year of cyber attacks, of which 337 required support and 80 were nationally significant.
The team also warned 8,500 organisations when their systems had been compromised by attackers, the report added.

articles.title_orig: UK will face AI cyberattacks on critical infrastructure by 2028, official says
articles.title_zh: UK will face AI cyberattacks on critical infrastructure by 2028, official says
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
The U.K. will likely face artificial intelligence cyberattacks on its critical infrastructure by 2028 as criminals and states, including China and Russia , increasingly use AI in their cyber activity, Britain 's cyber chief warned Tuesday.
That could include AI-powered malware for ransomware attacks as the technology will allow “vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long” to be discovered and exploited “at a scale that was once unimaginable,” Richard Horne, the head of the U.K.'s National Cyber Security Center said.
In a speech marking the publication of the NCSC's annual cyber report, Horne said the leaders of businesses and organizations of all sizes who have "got away with tech on the cheap" will have to explain why “food isn't on the shelves, lights aren't on, businesses have gone under,” if they fail to invest in cybersecurity or update out-of-date technology.
Chinese cyber activity is the “most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge facing the U.K.” while both Russia and China will routinely use AI to achieve their geopolitical goals, the report said. Russia is intentionally conducting cyber campaigns which fall below the threshold of armed conflict while Iran is carrying out attacks against the U.K. and targeting individuals who are a threat to the Iranian regime, Horne said.
The use of AI by states and criminals is highly likely to increase the scale and efficiency of hostile operations, but AI is more likely to be used to enhance and scale existing tactics and techniques rather than find brand new vulnerabilities, the report said.
Last week, governments and corporations worked on urgent security updates after the AI-assisted discovery of vulnerabilities in a programming language vital to 70% of websites globally. The two critical flaws identified by AI could allow bad actors to get unauthenticated access to sites which, in theory, could allow them to control a web server remotely without needing a password.
Technology “underpins the automation of physical processes that are vital to modern life,” Horne said. That includes, he said, electricity switching, sluice gates in water facilities, dam operations, manufacturing lines, heating and refrigeration controls. The recent cyberattacks on refrigeration systems in French supermarkets showed how easily hostile actors could exploit civilian infrastructure, Horne said.
Russia has already attacked critical infrastructure in Europe, according to the U.K. and EU member states that said Russia's FSB security service was behind an attack on Poland's energy grid in December 2025. If the attack had been successful, 500,000 people could have lost electricity during winter.
In the U.K., malicious cyber activity is costing organizations almost $20 billion every year, the NCSC said. In 2025, the carmaker Jaguar Land Rover suffered more than $260 million in direct losses following a cyberattack which also hit suppliers and dented the U.K. economy.
“We need every organization in the UK to take action now. Not only to protect their customers, services and livelihoods, but because cybersecurity is now part of the front line defense of our nation,” said Anne Keast-Butler, director of GCHQ, Britain’s signals intelligence agency, which the NCSC is part of.
That includes implementing basic but effective cybersecurity measures such as making sure devices are up to date, limiting administrator access to systems and backing up important files and data, the NCSC said.

articles.title_orig: Russia confirms new Ukraine peace talks as Melania Trump prepares to host ceasefire meeting
articles.title_zh: Russia confirms new Ukraine peace talks as Melania Trump prepares to host ceasefire meeting
articles.content_orig:
Russia on Tuesday confirmed that peace talks with Ukraine and the U.S. will go ahead next week in Abu Dhabi, while also signaling that a meeting between Presidents Vladimir Putin , Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to end the conflict was on the table.
Putin aide Vladimir ​Medinsky will serve ⁠as Moscow's chief negotiator ​at the talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a conference call, according to Reuters.
Separately, First Lady Melania Trump will bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives to the White House to discuss the local ceasefire in Kherson, the White House said Tuesday.
Monday saw the end of a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and surrounding areas in the Kherson region to allow for evacuation of residents, in a pause of hostilities that the White House said was brokered by the first lady.
Ukraine on Monday accused Russia of using the ceasefire to reinforce its military positions in the city.
The first lady's summit on Thursday will be "an extraordinary moment in American history," the White House said, but did not name the representatives who will attend. Melania Trump will deliver remarks on the Oleshky ceasefire at 11 a.m. ET Thursday, it added.
Peskov also said Tuesday the Kremlin hopes to finalize plans for a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, the U.S., and China in the coming days. The comments follow earlier reports that these countries were planning to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.
Zelenskyy has said that any negotiations over Ukraine's future must include Kyiv.
"It can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations," he said on Oct. 20, adding that he had discussed the proposal of a three-way meeting between the U.S., China, and Russia to negotiate an end to the nearly five-year full-scale war. "Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine," he said.
Tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine have mounted over recent weeks amid continued strikes between Moscow and Kyiv, including on civilian and energy targets.
A series of moves by the Trump administration in October raised questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner.
Tuesday's announcement follows U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff saying late Monday that Washington will mediate Ukraine-Russia peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, focusing on security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian issues.
Witkoff also said that U.S. negotiators will meet European and NATO officials in Brussels this week to discuss post-war security guarantees and Ukraine's reconstruction.

articles.title_orig: ‘Mogging’ is Collins’ word of the year, but what does it mean?
articles.title_zh: ‘Mogging’ is Collins’ word of the year, but what does it mean?
articles.content_orig:
Published: 04:59 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 08:42 EDT, 3 November 2026
It has been named the word of the year but you’d be forgiven for not having a clue what it means.
Mogging – meaning to outshine or dominate others – has been awarded the honour by the Collins English Dictionary thanks to a 210 per cent increase in its usage in 2026.
The word is said to be ‘fast-growing slang’ among Generation Z and Generation Alpha and was selected by lexicographers who analysed language use data online.
Not to be confused with ‘mugging’, some trace the origins of the term back to the acronym Amog – meaning Alpha Male of the Group – which has been used by online communities associated with the ‘manosphere’.
These forums focus on men’s issues such as masculinity and fitness but have been accused of promoting misogyny.
However, the term is now used more generally as a playful insult or compliment, depending on the situation.
The word has also risen in prominence following its use at last month's Conservative Party conference, after young attendees were spotted wearing badges bearing the word.
And, its rise has been championed by former Tory MP Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg – even if it is unrelated to his matching surname.
The former business secretary said mogging being named word of the year was 'excellent news' and will 'transmogrify our vocabulary'.
'Mogging' - meaning to dominate or outshine others - has been crowned the Collins English Dictionary's word of 2026
There has been a 210 per cent increase in the use of the term across 2026, which beat out words including 'carspreading' and 'Manchesterism'
He said: 'It is, in truth, mognificent, which I am expecting to be word of the year in 2027.'
Alex Beecroft, the Collins Dictionary's managing director, said 'mogging' was crowned winner after a consideration of 'patterns of usage' in words by lexicographers, as well as how 'often words are used'.
It beat terms including 'carspreading' and 'Manchesterism' to the top spot, which also experienced a boom in their use.
Mr Beecroft said the word was: 'a great example of how Gen Z and Gen Alpha have adopted a word and turned it into humorous slang, making the language their own and "mogging" the rest of us'.
He added: 'The selection of "mogging" as Collins' word of the year shows how each generation leaves its mark on language.'
'Manchesterism' has experienced a surge in use following the appointment of Mancunian Andy Burnham as Prime Minister, with the term describing his political philosophy.
'Carspreading' was also a frontrunner for the prize, referring to a pause in play used during matches at this summer's World Cup in the US.
Other popular terms included 'friendslop' a type of independent video game played as a team, and 'fricy', referring to foods and drinks which are simultaneously fruity and spicy.
'Bixie' was also highlighted as a contender, describing a women's haircut which is longer than a pixie cut but shorter than a bob.
Former Tory minister Jacob Rees-Mogg, whose surname bears a resemblance to the term, said it will 'transmogrify our vocabulary'
Last year, 'vibe coding' was selected as the dictionary's word of the year following an increase in use by Generation Z.
The term is defined as an easy way for people who struggle using technology to make computer code by telling artificial intelligence to do it.
Other words on the list last year included 'biohacking', defined as the activity of altering the natural processes of one's body in an attempt to improve health and longevity.
Another was 'clanker', a derogatory term for computers, robots , or sources of AI, which was popularised by a Star Wars TV series.
The word was commonly used on social media and is often used to express people's frustrations with, and distrust of, AI chatbots and platforms.
Also a term of disapproval, the word 'glaze' gained traction last year, meaning to praise or flatter someone excessively or undeservedly.
Another popular word was 'aura farming' – described as the deliberate cultivation of a distinctive and charismatic persona.
Last October, Dictionary.com also revealed its 2025 words of the year , with TikTok term '67' topping the list.
But according to the organisation, the definition of '67' remains complicated. It explained some people see it as a word that means, 'so–so', while some children view it as a way to annoy their parents.
What it means: To playfully outshine, outperform or update something or someone
What it means: A pause in play used during football matches
What it means: A way to quantify how cool someone is and whether they bring good energy. You can gain or lose aura points if you're being 'cringe'.
What it means:  Used to describe someone as a dominant leader, lone wolf, someone who is cool and popular.
You can also use it to say 'what the sigma' also translates to 'what the hell'.
What it means: Someone who has done exceptionally well or impressed others.
What it means: This can be used to convey that you like something or to describe someone's vibe or personality, for example, 'it's giving CEO,' which translates to: 'You are [or it is] giving CEO energy.'
What it means: Something is delicious or yummy.

articles.title_orig: Shopify Stock Plunges As Q3 Gross Operating Profit, Revenue Miss
articles.title_zh: Shopify Stock Plunges As Q3 Gross Operating Profit, Revenue Miss
articles.content_orig:
Shares of e-commerce platform Shopify fell 7% on Tuesday after the company missed estimates on subscription gross profit and gross merchandise volume.
Shopify reported before the bell Tuesday and posted adjusted earnings of 49 cents per share, topping LSEG estimates of 46 cents per share.
Overall, quarterly revenue of $3.74 billion came in just below LSEG estimates of $3.75 billion. Shopify said it sees revenue growth in the "low thirties" range year over year for the fourth quarter, versus LSEG estimates of 32.1%.
Gross merchandise volume, which came in at $119.15 billion, missed analyst estimates of $120.03 billion for the quarter, according to StreetAccount. Subscription gross profit also missed estimates by nearly $20 million, coming in at $661 million compared to StreetAccount estimates of $680.3 million. Merchant gross profit beat estimates.
Shopify president Harley Finkelstein called the GMV results "consistent" and "durable" in comments to CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Tuesday, and noted it was the thirteenth consecutive quarter of GMV growth above 20%.
"We're really proud of the print, and we're going to keep building for the long term and ignore the noise day to day," Finkelstein said.
Subscription revenue of $836 million also missed analyst estimates of $848.1 million, according to FactSet. Merchant revenue beat estimates.

This new PS5 version brings significant improvements over the original PS4 bundle of the two intense shooters, so they are worth revisiting again if you haven't already. Here's what to expect on PS5:
The third game in the series, Metro Exodus , was added to PS Plus Extra a few months ago, so now the entire franchise is playable natively on PS5 through Sony's subscription service. Now would also be a great time to catch up, with Metro 2039 out in February 2027.

articles.title_orig: Binance founder Changpeng Zhao addresses historic crypto hack: 'There's no 100% security'
articles.title_zh: Binance founder Changpeng Zhao addresses historic crypto hack: 'There's no 100% security'
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
It has been a busy few days for Changpeng Zhao in the wake of the hack on the enormous crypto platform he co-founded, Binance.
"It's been a pretty hectic process," Zhao, better known in crypto circles as CZ , told Yahoo Finance. "But the good thing is right now the withdrawals have been restored, the systems back to normal. People are free to use the platform without any issues now. And then all user funds are covered. The users did not suffer any loss."
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency trading platform and holds approximately $171 billion in total assets on its platform. The company is led by co-CEOs Richard Teng and Yi Le.
Hackers recently drained roughly $6.3 billion worth of digital assets from Binance on Oct. 29.
Here's what you need to know:
Blockchain intelligence firms and the FBI attributed the 20-minute raid with high confidence to TraderTraitor, an elite state-sponsored cyber unit tied to North Korea.
North Korea reportedly denied involvement.
Rather than cracking private cryptographic keys, the attackers reportedly breached internal automated transaction workflows via a Binance employee's laptop.
Read more: How to keep your crypto safe
Binance moved swiftly to stabilize the situation by guaranteeing full customer restitution, deploying corporate treasury reserves, Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) capital, and insurance funds to replenish user balances.
"There's no 100% security," CZ added. "So when you run a platform, especially a crypto platform the possibility is always there. I did not think it was going to be this big of magnitude, probably not."

articles.title_orig: Premier Tusk Says Poland Foiled Possible Provocation at Russia Border
articles.title_zh: Premier Tusk Says Poland Foiled Possible Provocation at Russia Border
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Poland has thwarted a potential Russian “provocation” on its border, according to the country’s prime minister Donald Tusk .
Tensions have been mounting between the countries over a series of issues including airspace violations and diplomatic disagreements as Europe remains concerned about a wider escalation from Moscow.
On Tuesday Polish police units were sent to the country’s border with the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad , Tusk said.
“We managed to prevent attempts at provocation – if that was indeed the intention,” he told reporters, according to France24.
He said that “individuals with flashlights” had been observed in the area, sparking concern.
“Just after midnight, I received information from the border guards that disturbing movement had been observed on the Polish-Russian border,” he said.
“We very quickly mobilised the appropriate forces and resources there and managed to prevent a provocation.”
The military, border guards and intelligence services had already been carrying out additional activities in the area to strengthen security.
A police spokesperson said that these preventive measures had been conducted in the northeastern regions of Warmia-Masuria and Podlaskie.
When authorities received “more precise” information about acts of sabotage including a potential incursion into Poland by “armed people” in the first half of November, additional police and troops were deployed as part of a special operation along the border regions on Tuesday, Tusk said.
“We have been receiving information for some time from our services and from allies' services that ... acts of diversion or more serious provocations on the border with Russia , or even sabotage acts orchestrated by hostile services, could occur,” he explained.
The Polish leader said he had also received warnings about possible escalations from Nato ’s supreme allied commander in Europe during his visit to Warsaw in October.
Tusk also accused Russia of trying to foment “instability” in Poland by meddling in a dispute between the government and the president over the Constitutional Tribunal.
President Karol Naworcki and Tusk have butted heads over the Tribunal leading to the suspension of the head of the court last week.
Russian politicians including Dmitry Medvedev, the deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, described Tusk’s government's moves in the dispute as “a coup”.
“We observe activity by Russia and pro-Russian politicians —both internationally and within the country, centring around our cause, which is defending the Constitutional Tribunal against aggressive behaviour by politicians and the demonstrators they provoke,” he said.
“We are all familiar with the Russian method of becoming involved in internal conflicts. Today, we are witnessing tensions provoked by the Russians, whether in connection with the midterm elections (in the US) or through the fuelling of a sense of instability (in Poland), based on the aggressive behaviour of opposition politicians and the president.”

articles.title_orig: Smugglers Bypass U.S. Controls to Ship HBM to China
articles.title_zh: Smugglers Bypass U.S. Controls to Ship HBM to China
articles.content_orig:
Despite U.S. export controls on advanced semiconductors to China, High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) produced by Samsung Electronics and SK hynix is reportedly being smuggled into China. Smugglers are using a method of packaging HBMs with low-end server processors to bypass export regulations, and then detaching only the memory once in China.
According to the U.S. IT media outlet The Information on Nov. 2 (local time), smugglers who have recently been siphoning Korean HBMs to China are exploiting loopholes in export regulations.
They package the HBM with a low-end server processor on a board and export it to China. They target the fact that while exporting HBM alone is subject to U.S. regulations, packaging it with a server processor classifies the package as a server processor item.
Under U.S. export regulations, the total computing power of a semiconductor package is evaluated based on the server processor, not the memory chip. The packages are disassembled upon arriving in China. Local technicians apply heat to the board to melt the solder, detach only the necessary HBM, and discard the remaining server processors.
The separation process requires highly sophisticated skills. It is reported that the failure rate is high because applying heat too quickly or for an extended period can cause the memory stack to warp or crack.
Nevertheless, the smuggling continues due to the massive profits.
A broker in his 20s who handles HBM smuggling in China told The Information that the price of a single HBM3E, which traded for several hundred dollars just a year ago, has recently soared to about $4,000. A single AI chip package requires 6 to 8 HBMs. The memory price alone amounts to $24,000 to $32,000. AI processors, servers, and power costs are separate.
The HBMs secured in this way are reportedly sold mainly to customers of Huawei, a Chinese telecommunications equipment and IT company.
According to sources familiar with Huawei’s supply chain, Huawei recently explained to some customers that its next-generation flagship AI chip, the Ascend 960DT, will largely be equipped with HBMs produced by Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. Huawei introduced that the performance of the Ascend 960DT is twice as superior as existing chips, and it will be one of the powerful processors that China can produce on its own.
As it became difficult to directly purchase the necessary memory chips from Korean companies, Huawei even advised some AI chip ordering customers to secure HBMs on their own. China is clinging to securing Korean HBMs because it lacks its own production capacity.
HBM is a core component that enhances the processing performance of AI processors by quickly transmitting large amounts of data. Without securing enough HBMs, it is difficult for a high-performance AI chip to exert its full performance even if it is developed. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix account for more than 80% of the global HBM market.
The problem is that such smuggling could also act as a burden on Korean semiconductor companies. Even if Samsung Electronics and SK hynix did not directly violate export control regulations, they could become targets of U.S. government surveillance if Chinese AI chips equipped with their memory are discovered.
In fact, Taiwan’s TSMC was investigated by the U.S. government in 2024 after semiconductors it produced were found in Huawei products. Subsequently, the U.S. ordered TSMC to completely halt AI chip exports to China.
SK hynix stated, “We are strictly complying with relevant laws and regulations, including the export control regulations of the U.S. and South Korea,” adding that it has never supplied products to Huawei since the implementation of U.S. export regulations in 2020.
Meanwhile, a perception is emerging among smugglers who consider their transactions to be a patriotic act.
A broker in his 20s who smuggles memory in China told The Information regarding his work, “It is contributing to the motherland.” He reportedly does not consider himself a smuggler.
However, as smuggling competition intensifies, concerns about crackdowns are also growing.
Another smuggler who has been ordering memory semiconductors from South Korea revealed that the risk of detection is increasing as other brokers have started using the transaction routes he used.
He said, “The more people like us there are, the easier it becomes to be discovered by regulatory authorities,” adding that he plans to sell most of his company stakes next year as crackdowns by South Korea and the U.S. are expected to be further strengthened in the future.

articles.title_orig: Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes
articles.title_zh: Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes
articles.content_orig:
Today's announcement has long been viewed in government as a potential political banana skin.
When the home secretary announced her first version of changes to the settlement system last year, many Labour MPs, including the housing secretary Angela Rayner, voiced their concerns about the plans.
But there was a feeling that Sir Keir Starmer's government was determined to plough on regardless. Shabana Mahmood herself repeatedly expressed how important she believed the reforms were.
But the change of prime minister over the summer gave renewed hope to those unhappy Labour MPs that they could force the Home Office into two changes.
Firstly, social care workers – under the original plans many social care workers would have had to wait 15 years before becoming eligible for settlement.
Secondly, the retrospective nature of the plans – some MPs were uncomfortable at the idea of someone coming to the UK and expecting to be eligible for settlement after five years, but then having to wait longer.
Angela Rayner described that as "un-British" and said the government shouldn't be shifting "the goalposts".
She returned to the cabinet under Andy Burnham as housing secretary and chose to repeat those criticisms in an interview during the Labour Party conference in September.
That was seen as evidence that a debate inside the top levels of government about whether to water down the plans was well and truly rumbling on.
For all the Labour MPs who wanted a change, there were others, particularly those in Brexit-supporting areas, who wanted the home secretary to stick the course.
Some inside government felt nervous about providing what they saw as catnip to Reform and the Conservatives.
All of that added up to one of the more difficult decisions that has had to be taken since Burnham walked through the doors of Number 10.
In the end ministers chose to water down the proposals for care workers – those who arrived before May 2025 and earn at least £25,000 a year will qualify for settlement in five years.
But the retrospective nature of the plans, the thing Rayner described as shifting "the goalposts", hasn't changed.
Despite that, the majority of Labour MPs pulled their punches when Mahmood made a statement in the House of Commons earlier .
Perhaps the strongest pushback came from Rachael Maskell, who is no fan of the retrospective element - but others on the left of the party, including John McDonnell and Diane Abbott, were critical without being scathing.
Outside the Commons chamber, the mood among Labour folk was pretty similar to what was said from the green benches.
One would-be critic said that while they personally still had concerns about the plans announced today, they believed the Home Secretary had successfully taken the political sting out of the situation for now.
They said the campaign by MPs and unions had led to a "big win" on settlement for social care workers, but said they were still expecting to hear from constituents negatively affected by the new rules.
One Number 10 source praised Mahmood's "take no prisoners" performance in the chamber, argued she had "found the right balance" and said the announcement had gone down as well as could be expected with Labour colleagues.
Of course, the home secretary will still need to deal with criticism from other parties.
Her opposite number for the Conservatives, Chris Philp, accused Mahmood of a significant U-turn.
Philp highlighted a claim she had previously made – that allowing care workers to reach settlement more quickly could cost the UK £10bn.
The social care workers plans announced today will see around 500,000 people have their path to settlement delayed , that number would have been around 800,000 under the original plans last year.
In an interview with the BBC, Mahmood wouldn't say what sort of financial burden her watering down would result in.
She also refused to confirm whether Burnham had directly asked her to water down the plans.
They are tricky questions that she will have to navigate over the coming weeks.
But the general view within government is that this is one political hurdle that has been successfully jumped.

articles.title_orig: US, Russia and China discuss trilateral meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi
articles.title_zh: US, Russia and China discuss trilateral meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi
articles.content_orig:
Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reports on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's response to Russian attacks, warning that strikes on their infrastructure will meet a painful response.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Monday that Russia is preparing a "massive attack" on Ukraine centered on Tuesday's midterm elections in the United States, accusing Moscow of seeking to exploit the historical vote to unleash strikes while the world's attention is elsewhere.
The Ukrainian leader's warning came as voters prepared to decide which party controls Congress, a result that could also influence Washington's future response to Russian President Vladimir Putin's almost five-year war in Ukraine.
In a post on X, Zelenskyy went on to urge the Trump administration to increase pressure on Moscow, warning that Russia could exploit the elections to target Ukraine's battered energy infrastructure and supply routes.
DRONE STRIKE SINKS SHIP IN NATO WATERS AS ZELENSKYY WARNS OF LOOMING ‘MASSIVE STRIKE’
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. (Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool Photo/Efrem Lukatsky/AP)
"We have intel that Russia is preparing a new massive attack on our country – primarily targeting energy and logistics," Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.
"The assumption is basically that tomorrow the world will be watching the American midterms, and what is happening here in Ukraine, along with our difficulties with air defense and Patriot missiles, will be overlooked."
Zelenskyy's warning came hours after Russian forces struck a school being used to distribute humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha, a settlement in southeastern Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region.
At least 26 people, including police officers and first responders, were killed, five others were injured and others remained missing, according to the Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda .
ZELENSKYY PRESSURES US AND EUROPE FOR MORE 'AIR DEFENSE' ASSISTANCE AMID ONGOING WAR WITH RUSSIA
Ukraine's largest private energy company reports 90% of generation capacity damaged by Russian attacks, leaving over 1 million without power during freezing temperatures. (Reuters)
In his X post, Zelenskyy urged the U.S. and its allies to warn Putin that continued attacks on Ukraine would bring serious economic consequences.
"We need signals from the world to Russia that will make them feel that terror is no good, that it will bring no gains, and that as long as this war continues, their oil will burn, and they will not be able to make money doing business with the world," Zelenskyy warned.
"We must not play games with Russia's oil or gas revenues," he added.
"We must put pressure on Russia in such a way that it has no alternative but to end this war. America can do this."
TRUMP ANNOUNCES IMMEDIATE ENERGY CEASEFIRE BETWEEN RUSSIA AND UKRAINE
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left talks with President Donald Trump and members of his Cabinet during a lunch meeting at the White House on Oct. 17, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has sought to negotiate an end to the war with the help of special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner , both of whom have been involved in diplomatic efforts with Moscow.
Zelenskyy told Fox News in a Sunday interview that Ukraine would suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries for a month if Washington provided Patriot missile interceptors during the same period, potentially opening the door to diplomacy.
The State Department approved the potential sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptor missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion, according to Reuters.
The proposed sale could provide a significant boost to Ukraine's air defenses if finalized, although the delivery timeline is uncertain.
TRUMP SAYS US WILL LET UKRAINE MAKE PATRIOT MISSILES IN MAJOR POLICY SHIFT
First Lady Melania Trump, left, and civilians being evacuated from Oleshky, Ukraine, in October 2022 during the early days of the Russia-Ukraine war. (Umit Bektas/Reuters; Alexander Ermochenko/Reuters)
On Monday, Ukraine also accused Moscow of exploiting a U.S.-backed humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky , in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, to strengthen Russian military positions.
Nearly 800 people were evacuated during the six-day humanitarian pause, according to first lady Melania Trump, with the White House clarifying that she helped broker the arrangement.
Ukraine's General Staff accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian pause to rotate troops, reinforce their defenses and improve battlefield logistics.
"Under the ceasefire introduced for the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, units of the Defence Forces of Ukraine ensured that the ceasefire was observed and acted exclusively within the framework of the agreements reached," the General Staff said in a statement on X.

"The enemy, by contrast, used the humanitarian pause to improve its positions."
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

Those travelling from Hangzhou or Wuhan can have bags checked through to final destination overseas under new one-stop service launched on Tuesday
Travellers flying from Hangzhou or Wuhan to overseas destinations via Hong Kong on different airlines can have their baggage checked through to the final destination under a newly launched service that aims to step up the connections between mainland Chinese cities and other countries.
Under the new one-stop service that launched on Tuesday, travellers departing from Hangzhou Xiaoshan International Airport or Wuhan Tianhe International Airport will not need to check in their baggage again when transferring through Hong Kong, even if they are flying on a different airline on the next leg of their journey.
“Hong Kong International Airport is launching a game-changing service,” Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said.

articles.title_orig: Asian trading is mixed as tech sell-off deepens and oil prices rebound
articles.title_zh: Asian trading is mixed as tech sell-off deepens and oil prices rebound
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Oil prices tumbled more than seven percent on Monday, the eve of crucial midterm elections in the United States, as signals that Tehran and Washington were renewing dialogue boosted hopes of ending the Middle East war.
Iran on Monday said "intensive" exchanges were underway with Washington and offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under strict conditions, as efforts escalated to avert a return to conflict.
Earlier, the Axios news outlet reported that US Vice President JD Vance had sent a letter to Iranian national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about possible new talks.
That was the highest-level move from President Donald Trump's administration in months.
Again Capital's John Kilduff described investors as experiencing "a violent change in market sentiment," adding that "we went from really, I think, expecting a major offensive after tomorrow's US elections to a potential breakthrough," he told AFP.
"All these losses will be taken right back if this doesn't pan out," Kilduff said.
The steep drop in oil prices translated into weakness among petroleum stocks. But Wall Street shares otherwise began the day with promise, bouncing back after last Friday's rout precipitated by worries over the tech industry's massive artificial intelligence spending.
But tech shares came under pressure as the session progressed, with the tech-focused Nasdaq slumping 1.1 percent.
"This is still a market that is on edge," said Joseph Zidle, chief market strategist at Cresset Capital, who described unease about midterm elections as adding to worries about the AI boom.
"The two of them are actually related," Zidle said of midterms and AI, noting that opposition to data centers has animated many campaigns.
AI has been "on the ballot in so many places, both blue and red," Zidle said. "It seems like data centers are part of the kitchen table issues."
Pollsters expect Democrats to win back control of the House of Representatives, but view Trump's Republican party as potentially able to maintain a majority in the Senate.
The loss of total Republican dominance would push the president into unfamiliar and uncomfortable territory: a lame duck period beset with high inflation at home, the sputtering war against Iran and hostile Democratic investigations into his activities in Washington.
"Investors are bracing for a fresh round of turbulence ahead of US midterm election fireworks while they assess the extent that companies are burning through cash to keep the AI bonfires burning," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.
Earnings this week will come from Apple, which reports after the close of trading on Monday, as well as Advanced Micro Devices and software titan Palantir will be closely watched this week. Shares in Apple fell 1.8 percent.

articles.title_orig: Blackstone president calls for more equity to fund AI buildout as debt risks mount
articles.title_zh: Blackstone president calls for more equity to fund AI buildout as debt risks mount
articles.content_orig:
The artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout will need more equity financing as lenders become increasingly exposed to the companies driving the buildout, Blackstone President Jon Gray said Tuesday.
Speaking at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit, Gray said the scale of capital required for AI is creating concentration risks for debt investors, both across the sector and at individual companies.
Unlike shareholders, who can benefit from a company's growth, lenders have limited upside as their returns are largely confined to interest and principal repayments, he said.
Speaking at the same panel, Pimco CEO Emmanuel Roman warned investors that the scale of AI financing could prove to be "too much" for markets to absorb.
Roman said AI-related capital spending could reach around $10 trillion over the next five years, citing General Atlantic CEO Bill Ford's estimate. He added that about $550 billion in AI debt had been issued in various forms so far this year.
Even with a mix of equity and debt financing, the amount required would be “gigantic,” Roman said, comparing it with a global corporate bond market of roughly $20 trillion.
“At some point in time, it’s going to be too much,” he said.
Global data center demand will require about $8.5 trillion in capital spending over the next five years, Goldman Sachs wrote in a report Monday.
Gray said financing the buildout would require a combination of public markets, banks and private capital, with companies increasingly turning to structured transactions to limit the amount of debt they take on. Cash generated by hyperscalers would also fund part of the spending, he said.
“The creativity is needed because the scale of capital is enormous," Gray said.
Despite those financing challenges, Gray remained bullish on AI infrastructure, saying demand for computing power was “running well ahead of supply.”
Spending on AI models across Blackstone’s portfolio companies had risen 20-fold over the past year as businesses saw financial benefits from uses including coding, customer engagement and content creation, he said.
Meeting that demand remains difficult, however, as securing sites, permits, chips, power and capital becomes more challenging, according to Gray.

articles.title_orig: North Korea denies being behind $6.3bn Binance crypto hack
articles.title_zh: North Korea denies being behind $6.3bn Binance crypto hack
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".
Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un , said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.
This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.
Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.
The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.
"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.
"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.
But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.
The country has consistently denied such claims.
Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".
Binance did not respond to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.
Since the incident, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users.
The company's spokesperson said that a net $4.72bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed on Sunday.
The net outflow represents a "relatively limited portion"  of Binance's total assets, which stand at approximately $157bn, the spokesperson told the BBC on Tuesday.
That figure reflects the impact of the hack, subsequent withdrawals and market price changes.
"Withdrawal levels are stabilising to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity," she added.
The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals.
Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.
The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach.
